chapters.title: The atmosphere and aerodynamic forces
chapters.summary: Aircraft fly through an atmosphere whose pressure, density and temperature fall with altitude in a standardised way. Every aerodynamic force comes from pressure and shear acting on the surface, and dimensional analysis compresses their dependence on speed, size and air properties into a few coefficients and two numbers — Reynolds and Mach. Measuring airspeed with a pitot tube and correcting it for altitude completes the toolkit.

items.name: The International Standard Atmosphere
items.pic: Climb through the standard atmosphere with an altitude slider: temperature falls linearly in the troposphere then stays constant in the stratosphere, while pressure and density decay, all integrated live from hydrostatics.

items.name: Aerodynamic forces from pressure and shear
items.pic: Around an airfoil, pressure arrows and skin-friction arrows are drawn along the surface; their vector sum is resolved into lift and drag, and switching off one contribution shows which dominates.

items.name: Lift, drag and moment coefficients
items.pic: Change speed, air density and wing area for the same shape and angle: the forces vary widely, but divided by dynamic pressure and area they collapse to the same coefficients.

items.name: Similarity: Reynolds and Mach numbers
items.pic: Scale a wind-tunnel model and its test speed: the tool shows whether Reynolds and Mach numbers both match the full-size aircraft, and why it is usually impossible to match both at once.

items.name: Airspeed measurement: indicated and true airspeed
items.pic: A pitot-static probe reads the same dynamic pressure at sea level and at altitude for different true speeds; the indicated and true airspeeds are displayed as the altitude slider rises.

items.name: Speed of sound and Mach number
items.pic: A pressure pulse propagates through air at a temperature set by the user: its speed √(γRT) is read out, and the Mach number of a cruising jet changes with altitude even at fixed true speed.

chapters.title: Airfoils
chapters.summary: An airfoil's job is to turn the oncoming flow and so produce lift with little drag. Its lift grows almost linearly with angle of attack at a rate close to 2π per radian until the flow separates and the wing stalls. The aerodynamic centre, where the pitching moment stays constant, organises the moment data; pressure distributions, panel methods and high-lift devices show how designers predict and shape the flow.

items.name: Airfoil geometry: camber, thickness and angle of attack
items.pic: Edit a four-digit airfoil with sliders for camber, camber position and thickness; the shape, chord line and mean camber line update, and the angle of attack rotates the oncoming flow.

items.name: The lift curve and stall
items.pic: Sweep the angle of attack: lift coefficient follows a straight line of slope near 2π per radian, with an offset set by camber, then peaks and drops as separation spreads forward from the trailing edge.

items.name: Pressure coefficient distribution
items.pic: Plot the pressure coefficient over upper and lower surfaces: the area between the two curves is the lift coefficient, and the suction peak near the leading edge sharpens with angle of attack.

items.name: Centre of pressure and aerodynamic centre
items.pic: As angle of attack changes, the centre of pressure wanders along the chord, while the moment about the quarter-chord point stays constant, marked as the aerodynamic centre.

items.name: Panel methods
items.pic: Cover an arbitrary airfoil with source and vortex panels: solving for their strengths gives the surface velocity and lift, which converge to the exact Joukowski result as panels are added.

items.name: High-lift devices: flaps and slats
items.pic: Deploy flaps and slats: the lift curve shifts up and the stall angle changes, and the minimum landing speed computed from the new maximum lift coefficient drops.

items.name: Airfoil drag: friction and pressure drag
items.pic: Change the Reynolds number and the transition point: skin-friction drag falls with Reynolds number, jumps when the boundary layer turns turbulent, and pressure drag rises when separation grows.

chapters.title: Wings and drag
chapters.summary: A finite wing leaks air around its tips, shedding a vortex wake that tilts the lift backward and creates induced drag, a cost of lift itself. Aspect ratio and span loading control it, and the combination with friction and pressure drag gives the drag polar — the single curve that governs aircraft performance. Lifting-line theory, vortex lattices, ground effect and formation flight all follow from the same vortex picture.

items.name: Wingtip vortices and downwash
items.pic: Smoke particles released behind a finite wing roll up into two counter-rotating tip vortices; the downwash they induce at the wing is plotted along the span.

items.name: Induced drag and aspect ratio
items.pic: Stretch a wing to a higher aspect ratio at fixed area: the induced drag at a given lift falls as 1/AR, plotted from C_L²/(πeAR) and compared with a lifting-line computation.

items.name: Elliptic loading minimises induced drag
items.pic: Draw any spanwise lift distribution with the mouse at fixed total lift: the induced drag readout is smallest when the distribution is elliptical, and the span efficiency e drops for other shapes.

items.name: Vortex-lattice method
items.pic: Model a swept or tapered wing as a grid of horseshoe vortices: solving for their strengths gives the spanwise lift distribution and induced drag, which can be compared for different planforms.

items.name: The drag polar
items.pic: Plot drag coefficient against lift coefficient: a parabola C_D = C_D0 + K C_L² whose two parts are shaded; tangents from the origin locate the best lift-to-drag ratio.

items.name: Maximum L/D: induced drag equals parasite drag
items.pic: Slide the flight speed: parasite drag rises as V² and induced drag falls as 1/V², and their sum is smallest exactly where the two curves cross.

items.name: Ground effect
items.pic: Lower a wing toward the ground: an image vortex system below the surface weakens the downwash, and the induced drag reduction is plotted against height over span.

items.name: Formation flight: geese in a V
items.pic: Position birds behind and beside one another: each bird in the upwash of its neighbour’s tip vortex needs less power, and the total saving is maximised near a tip-overlap V formation.

chapters.title: Compressibility and high-speed flight
chapters.summary: As flight speed approaches the speed of sound, air compresses noticeably: pressure coefficients grow, local supersonic regions appear and shock waves bring a steep rise in drag. Simple corrections handle subsonic compressibility, swept wings and the area rule delay the drag rise, and in supersonic flow oblique shocks and expansion fans replace smooth turning. At hypersonic speeds, heating becomes the dominant design problem.

items.name: Prandtl–Glauert compressibility correction
items.pic: Scale an incompressible panel pressure calculation by 1/√(1 − M²), retain its complete pressure range, and compare its suction peak with the sonic threshold. Their intersection estimates where the subsonic approximation fails.

items.name: Critical Mach number and drag divergence
items.pic: Compare the pressure-based sonic-onset diagnostic with an independent Korn/Lock drag correlation. Technology changes the engineering correlation while the chosen NACA section stays fixed; neither calculation locates a shock.

items.name: Swept wings delay drag divergence
items.pic: Resolve velocity into perpendicular and spanwise projections for a cylindrical-wing argument, then compare its cosine estimate with a separate swept-strip correlation. Leading-edge and half-chord sweep are identified separately.

items.name: The area rule
items.pic: Plot the cross-sectional area of an aircraft along its length: smoothing that distribution by pinching the fuselage at the wing reduces wave drag, compared for a straight and a “coke-bottle” fuselage.

items.name: Oblique shocks and Prandtl–Meyer expansion
items.pic: Turn a supersonic stream with a wedge or a corner: a compression corner makes an oblique shock whose angle is computed from the turning angle and Mach number, while an expansion corner makes a fan of Mach waves.

items.name: Supersonic thin-airfoil theory (Ackeret)
items.pic: For a thin flat plate or diamond airfoil at supersonic speed, the pressure on each face depends only on its local slope; lift and wave drag coefficients are computed and compared with shock-expansion results.

items.name: Hypersonic aerodynamic heating
refs: NASA TR R-376; NASA TFAWS2012 Aerothermodynamics Course, Lecture1 slides17,28–29
items.pic: Vary density, effective nose radius, emissivity and speed; compute the Earth-air stagnation-point convective correlation and a separate radiation-balance reference, with a button reproducing the NASA course example.

items.name: Drag-Rise Characteristics of Wing-Body Combinations

paper.title: A Study of the Zero-Lift Drag-Rise Characteristics of Wing-Body Combinations Near the Speed of Sound

refs: Whitcomb1952, complete original report, Tables I–III and Figure10
items.pic: Compare the basic, equivalent and indented body radii from Whitcomb’s original geometry tables, then inspect the reported approximate near-sonic reduction of the wing-associated drag-rise increment for each cylindrical-body case.

chapters.title: Aircraft performance
chapters.summary: Force, energy and fuel balances for chosen aircraft models, with explicit engine laws, stall constraints and numerical validity boundaries.

items.name: Steady level flight
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §A, steady level force/polar equations
items.pic: Change weight, geometric altitude and speed. The curves separate the two drag terms; a feasible request shows the four balanced forces. An out-of-polar request is marked explicitly and its force illustration is omitted.

items.name: Minimum-drag and minimum-power speeds
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §§A–B, minimum drag and power equations
items.pic: Move the weight, ISA altitude and lift limit. Both unconstrained optima and the admissible optima are marked separately on drag and power curves. Tightening the lift limit can put either optimum at the stall boundary.

items.name: Gliding flight: glide ratio equals L/D
refs: MIT16.687 Aircraft Performance, PDF p4 slide7; own resolved-force derivation
items.pic: Choose a lift coefficient and release height. The descent path, angle, speed and horizontal range use one exact force triangle. The second panel finds best glide ratio; a coefficient above the chosen lift limit produces no admissible glide path.

items.name: Rate of climb from excess power
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §E, energy balance and propulsive efficiency
items.pic: Vary speed, shaft power and efficiency. The actual propulsive-power gap and estimated climb rate recompute together. The energy ledger divides the selected available power into aerodynamic dissipation and potential-energy flux.

items.name: Absolute and service ceilings
refs: MIT16.687 Aircraft Performance, PDF p13 slide25; independently derived chosen density-lapse model
items.pic: Change sea-level available power and its chosen density exponent. Move through the actual ISA profile and compare the absolute root with a declared0.508m/s service threshold. Missing roots remain missing, rather than becoming endpoint altitudes.

items.name: Breguet range equation
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §C, weight ODE/logarithm; coefficient convention explicitly defined here
items.pic: Change speed, lift/drag ratio, the explicitly defined fuel coefficient and fuel fraction. The logarithmic range curve and normalized exponential burn history use the same schedule; the readout gives both range and time, including exact zero fuel.

items.name: Breguet endurance
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §§B–D, read with explicit engine-specific fuel laws; own derivative comparison
items.pic: Switch the engine law and change weight, altitude or the lift limit. Two separately normalized curves show fuel per time and per distance, with their constrained optima. A maximum-range speed is not universally a minimum-drag speed.

items.name: Turning flight, load factor and the V–n diagram
refs: Own resolved-force derivation from written Newton law and5.1; no airframe envelope table
items.pic: Change bank, speed and the chosen structural bound. A unit-radius map shows the geometry of a feasible turn; the envelope panel shows the actual load request and its stall/structure limits. Zero bank gives a straight path, while an infeasible request has no displayed turn path.

items.name: Takeoff and landing distances
refs: MIT16.687 Aircraft Performance PDF p15, ground-roll/obstacle distinction; own chosen-force integration
items.pic: Switch between the two explicitly chosen ground-roll laws and vary weight, density, thrust or braking. The speed–distance curve comes from the actual force integral, alongside net force versus speed. Unreachable takeoff and zero-braking landing remain separate states, not capped fake distances.

items.name: The back side of the power curve
refs: MIT Unified Propulsion IV §§B/E; own scalar-law derivative and mean-value stability proof
items.pic: Switch constant power versus constant thrust at the same trim speed. The phase curve and actual integrated deviation growth show why a speed between Vp and Vd can have opposite local behavior under the two laws. Change the initial signed perturbation, including exact zero.

chapters.title: Stability and control
chapters.summary: An aircraft is statically stable in pitch if a nose-up disturbance produces a nose-down moment, which depends on where the centre of gravity sits relative to the neutral point. Dynamically, its motion splits into a handful of characteristic modes — the slow phugoid, the quick short-period oscillation, the Dutch roll and the spiral — whose eigenvalues pilots feel as handling qualities. Fly-by-wire and aeroelasticity show where control theory and structures meet the airframe.

items.name: Longitudinal static stability
items.pic: Plot pitching moment against angle of attack for the whole aircraft: a negative slope pushes the nose back after a gust, and moving the centre of gravity aft flattens the slope.

items.name: Neutral point and static margin
items.pic: Slide the centre of gravity along the fuselage: the static margin to the neutral point is displayed, and the trimmed aircraft becomes unstable when the centre of gravity passes it.

items.name: Trim and the role of the horizontal tail
items.pic: Adjust tail incidence or elevator angle until the total pitching moment is zero at the desired lift coefficient; the trim point slides along the moment curve.

items.name: The phugoid mode
items.pic: Disturb an aircraft’s speed: it trades altitude and speed back and forth in a long, lightly damped oscillation whose period is close to Lanchester’s π√2 V/g.

items.name: The short-period mode
items.pic: Pulse the elevator: angle of attack and pitch rate respond in a fast, well-damped oscillation, and the linearised model’s eigenvalues are plotted beside the phugoid pair.

items.name: Directional (weathercock) stability
items.pic: Yaw an aircraft with a gust: the vertical fin produces a restoring moment like a weathervane, and shrinking the fin until the yawing-moment slope changes sign makes the aircraft diverge.

items.name: Lateral modes: roll subsidence, spiral and Dutch roll
items.pic: Perturb the lateral motion: the eigenvalues of the lateral equations split into a fast roll mode, a slow spiral mode and an oscillatory Dutch roll, each animated on a model aircraft.

items.name: Dihedral effect
items.pic: Raise the wing dihedral: a sideslip now produces a restoring roll moment, which stabilises the spiral mode but makes the Dutch roll worse, shown by eigenvalues moving as dihedral changes.

items.name: Relaxed static stability and fly-by-wire
items.pic: Move the centre of gravity behind the neutral point to cut trim drag: the bare airframe diverges, but a feedback controller on pitch rate places the closed-loop poles back in the stable region.

items.name: Flutter
items.pic: A wing section with bending and twisting springs sits in an airflow: as speed rises the two modes’ frequencies approach, merge, and a growing oscillation sets in at the flutter speed.

items.name: Some Aeronautical Experiments

paper.title: Some Aeronautical Experiments
paper.venue: Journal of the Western Society of Engineers, December 1901 (address of 18 September 1901)

items.pic: Fly the Wrights’ glider: twist the wing tips to restore lateral balance instead of shifting the pilot’s body, trim with the forward elevator, and compare the lift actually obtained in a measured wind with the lift promised by Lilienthal’s tables, as Wilbur reported.

chapters.title: Propulsion
chapters.summary: Every engine that flies makes thrust by throwing mass backward faster than it came in. The thrust equation and the propulsive efficiency explain why big slow jets beat small fast ones, and actuator-disk momentum theory covers propellers and rotors. Turbojets, turbofans and ramjets follow from the Brayton cycle, and rockets — which carry their own propellant — are characterised by specific impulse and their nozzles' expansion.

items.name: The thrust equation
items.pic: Draw a control volume around an engine: thrust equals the net momentum flux out plus the pressure imbalance at the exit, with sliders for mass flow, exit velocity and exit pressure.

items.name: Propulsive efficiency: 2/(1 + V_e/V)
items.pic: Produce the same thrust with a small fast jet or a large slow one: the kinetic energy wasted in the wake is shaded, and the efficiency curve rises as exhaust speed approaches flight speed.

items.name: Actuator-disk momentum theory
items.pic: A propeller is replaced by a thin disk that adds pressure: the stream tube contracts through it, and the velocity at the disk is exactly halfway between the upstream and far-wake speeds.

items.name: Hovering rotor: induced power
items.pic: Hover a helicopter with adjustable rotor diameter and weight: the ideal power T^{3/2}/√(2ρA) is computed, showing why large rotors and dense air make hovering cheaper.

items.name: The turbojet and the ideal Brayton cycle
items.pic: Follow air through compressor, combustor, turbine and nozzle on a pressure–volume and temperature–entropy diagram; raising the compressor pressure ratio increases cycle efficiency.

items.name: Turbofans and bypass ratio
items.pic: Increase the bypass ratio: more air is accelerated less, propulsive efficiency rises and fuel consumption falls, with the engine cross-section growing to match.

items.name: Ramjets and scramjets
items.pic: Raise the flight Mach number: ram compression alone replaces the compressor above about Mach 2, and above Mach 5 combustion must happen in supersonic flow to avoid excessive heating.

items.name: Specific impulse
items.pic: Compare engines by impulse delivered per weight of propellant: solid, kerosene–oxygen, hydrogen–oxygen and ion engines are placed on a bar chart of specific impulse in seconds.

items.name: Rocket nozzles and expansion ratio
items.pic: Change the nozzle’s area ratio at different ambient pressures: thrust peaks when the exhaust is expanded to ambient pressure, and over-expanded flow at sea level shows shock diamonds.

chapters.title: Rockets
chapters.summary: A rocket's velocity change depends only on its exhaust speed and the logarithm of its mass ratio — a deceptively simple law with harsh consequences. Reaching orbit takes about 9 km/s once gravity and drag losses are paid, which forces staging; optimising the stages is a constrained optimisation problem. Electric propulsion trades thrust for exhaust speed and opens a different region of mission design.

items.name: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation
items.pic: Burn propellant out of a rocket in small packets: the accumulated velocity change converges to v_e ln(m₀/m_f), with sliders for exhaust speed and mass ratio.

items.name: The tyranny of the rocket equation
items.pic: Ask for more Δv: the required mass ratio grows exponentially and the payload fraction of a single-stage rocket shrinks toward zero, plotted on a log scale.

items.name: The Δv budget to orbit: gravity and drag losses
items.pic: Fly a launch simulation: Δv spent is split into orbital speed, gravity losses that grow with slow climbs, and drag losses that grow with fast low-altitude flight, as stacked bars.

items.name: Staging
items.pic: Split a rocket into two or three stages that drop empty tanks: the achievable Δv for the same total mass rises sharply, with the mass of each stage shown as a stacked bar.

items.name: Optimal staging
items.pic: Choose how to divide Δv among stages: the payload fraction is plotted over the split, and the Lagrange-multiplier optimum is marked and confirmed by brute-force search.

items.name: The gravity turn
items.pic: Pitch a rocket slightly just after launch and let gravity bend its trajectory toward horizontal at zero angle of attack; the kick angle slider determines whether it reaches orbit, falls back, or overshoots.

items.name: Electric propulsion: low thrust, high specific impulse
items.pic: An ion engine spirals a spacecraft slowly outward over months; for a fixed power supply, increasing exhaust speed reduces thrust, and the mission time and propellant mass trade off.

items.name: Optimal exhaust speed for power-limited propulsion
items.pic: For a power-limited spacecraft, plot delivered payload against exhaust speed: too slow wastes propellant, too fast wastes power, and the optimum scales with the required Δv.

items.name: Exploration of Cosmic Space by Means of Reaction Devices

paper.title: Исследование мировых пространств реактивными приборами (The Exploration of Cosmic Space by Means of Reaction Devices)

items.pic: Burn propellant from a rocket of adjustable mass ratio and exhaust speed and watch the velocity follow v = c ln(M₀/M₁); a table of final speeds for growing mass ratios sits beside the curve, with orbital and escape speeds marked.

items.name: A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes

paper.title: A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes

items.pic: Choose a target altitude, exhaust speed and drag, and the simulation finds the minimum starting mass per pound lifted, the steep curve of Goddard’s tables; a nozzle panel shows how a converging–diverging nozzle raised the exhaust speed he measured.

chapters.title: Orbital mechanics and manoeuvres
chapters.summary: Spacecraft move on Keplerian conics between impulsive burns, so mission design is the art of choosing burns. The vis-viva equation turns every manoeuvre into arithmetic, and the Hohmann transfer is the cheapest two-burn route between circular orbits — except when a three-burn bi-elliptic transfer wins. Plane changes are costly, burns deep in a gravity well are efficient (the Oberth effect), and gravity assists and low-energy routes borrow energy from planets and three-body dynamics.

items.name: Classical orbital elements
items.pic: Six sliders — semi-major axis, eccentricity, inclination, node, argument of periapsis, true anomaly — place an orbit and a satellite in 3D around a globe.

items.name: Circular and escape velocity
items.pic: Launch horizontally from a mountain with increasing speed: the trajectories pass from falling back, to a circle, to ellipses, to the parabola at √2 times circular speed, to hyperbolas.

items.name: Kepler’s equation and time of flight
items.pic: Pick a time after periapsis: Kepler’s equation is solved by Newton iteration for the eccentric anomaly, and the satellite is placed on its orbit with the swept area shaded.

items.name: The Hohmann transfer
items.pic: Raise a satellite from a low circular orbit to a high one with two tangential burns; the Δv of each burn and the transfer time are read out as the target radius slider moves.

items.name: Bi-elliptic transfer beats Hohmann at large radius ratios
items.pic: Compare total Δv for Hohmann and bi-elliptic transfers against the ratio of final to initial radius: the bi-elliptic curve dips below once the ratio exceeds about 11.94, at the cost of much longer flight time.

items.name: Plane changes are expensive
items.pic: Rotate an orbit’s plane by a chosen angle: the required Δv is 2v sin(Δi/2), compared with combining the plane change with a Hohmann burn at apoapsis where the speed is low.

items.name: The Oberth effect
items.pic: Fire the same Δv burn at periapsis and at apoapsis of an eccentric orbit: the gain in orbital energy (v·Δv per unit mass) is far larger at periapsis, as the escape speeds afterward show.

items.name: Spheres of influence and patched conics
items.pic: An interplanetary trajectory is pieced together from a departure hyperbola, a heliocentric ellipse and an arrival hyperbola; the sphere-of-influence boundaries are drawn where one conic hands over to the next.

items.name: Gravity assists
items.pic: Fly past a moving planet: in its frame the flyby only rotates the velocity, but in the Sun’s frame the spacecraft gains or loses speed depending on which side it passes, with velocity triangles drawn.

items.name: Synodic period and launch windows
items.pic: Earth and Mars circle the Sun: the phase angle needed for a Hohmann transfer recurs every synodic period, about 26 months, and missed windows are counted on a timeline.

items.name: Lambert’s problem
items.pic: Pick two positions and a flight time: the unique conic connecting them is found by iteration, and a porkchop plot of Δv over departure and arrival dates is built from many Lambert solutions.

items.name: Rendezvous: the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations
items.pic: Approach a space station from a nearby orbit: in the station’s rotating frame, thrusting toward it makes the chaser drift up and behind, and the linear relative-motion solution predicts the looping path.

items.name: Speed up to slow down: the orbital phasing paradox
items.pic: To catch a satellite ahead of you, burning forward raises your orbit and slows your average angular speed so you fall further behind; braking first is what closes the gap, as the phasing simulation shows.

items.name: Oblateness: nodal precession and Sun-synchronous orbits
items.pic: Earth’s equatorial bulge makes an inclined orbit’s plane precess; tune the inclination of a low orbit until the precession matches one turn per year, keeping the orbit fixed relative to the Sun.

items.name: Geostationary orbit
items.pic: Raise a circular equatorial orbit until its period equals one sidereal day: the satellite then hovers over a fixed point on the rotating globe, at about 35,786 km altitude.

items.name: Low-energy transfers and Lagrange-point orbits
items.pic: In the rotating Earth–Moon frame, a spacecraft follows a halo orbit around L1 and then slips along its unstable manifold toward the Moon with almost no fuel, compared with a direct transfer.

chapters.title: Entry and attitude
chapters.summary: Coming home means shedding orbital energy in the atmosphere, where the trajectory, the peak deceleration and the heating depend on the vehicle's ballistic coefficient and shape — blunt bodies survive by pushing the hot shock layer away. In orbit, spacecraft must also point: spin, gravity gradients and momentum wheels each stabilise attitude, and energy dissipation decides which spin axis is truly stable.

items.name: Ballistic entry and peak deceleration
items.pic: Enter the atmosphere at a chosen flight-path angle: deceleration peaks at an altitude set by the ballistic coefficient, but its maximum value depends only on entry speed and angle.

items.name: Blunt-body principle for entry heating
items.pic: Compare a sharp cone and a blunt capsule entering at the same speed: the blunt body’s detached shock dumps most of the energy into the air, and its nose heating rate is far lower.

items.name: Spin stability and energy dissipation (Explorer 1)
items.pic: Spin a satellite about its long (minimum-inertia) axis with flexible antennas that dissipate energy: the spin slowly turns into a tumble about the maximum-inertia axis, as the first US satellite did.

items.name: Gravity-gradient stabilisation
items.pic: A long satellite in orbit is pulled by tidal torque to point its long axis at the Earth, and librates about that attitude after a disturbance.

items.name: Reaction wheels and momentum dumping
items.pic: Spin up an internal wheel to rotate the spacecraft the other way; external torques gradually saturate the wheel, which must be unloaded with thrusters or magnetorquers.

items.name: Motion and Aerodynamic Heating of Ballistic Missiles

paper.authors: H. Julian Allen and A. J. Eggers, Jr.
paper.title: A Study of the Motion and Aerodynamic Heating of Ballistic Missiles Entering the Earth’s Atmosphere at High Supersonic Speeds

items.pic: Send entry bodies of adjustable ballistic coefficient into an exponential atmosphere: the peak deceleration of a steep entry is the same whatever the mass, and the share of heat reaching the body falls as the nose is made blunter.
